12: The Explanation of the Word 'Anava' (Humility) and its Qualities:  To explain humility, we refer to one who is 'Ani' (poor) and 'Inui' (tortured) in a way that he is surrendered.  It is the concept of being poor and dependant [meaning, he will accept anything that comes his way].  So too (as in Parshat Shemot 10:3), "מאנת לענות מפני," from the Targaminan, "לאתכנעא."  So too, this applies to a poor person and one who is fasting, as it says, "וכי התענית בכל אשר התענה אבי," and from this we can take that in all of these, the intention of them is the level of surrender.

And here, with the concept of surrender, the humble [person] finds himself with the the Creator - Hashem.  Just as He is elevated above all of those elevated, and 'gaah' above all of those who are 'gaim', just as we said with what was written (in Tehillim, chapter 33:1), "ה' מלך גאות לבש."  So too [we find humility] with Dovid haMelech (alav haShalom) (in Tehillim, chapter 18:36), "וענותך תרבני," as it is explained in Midrash Tanchuma (ילקוט שמואל רמז קסא) about this passuk.  This is what it says.  "With my right [hand], I support you," (Tehillim 18:36) -- this is what is written in the Torah, "מימינו אש דת למו" (Devarim 33:2).  And, "Your humility is multiplied," as in, who is humble like Hashem?  A person says to his friend: Come and beautify the brides, or visit the sick, or bury the dead, or give comfort to the mourners: and he says to him, "I am a 'gadol' and rich; why should I go [and do these]?  However, Hashem [does each of these, as it is written in these pasukim]:  ויבן את הצלע (Bereishit 22:2), וירא אליו ה' (Devarim 18:1), ויקבור אותו בגי (Devarim 34:6), וירא אלהים אל יעקב (Bereishit 25:9).

Rabbi Abba bar Acha said, a student sits to learn before his Rav, and he says, "I strived."  However, Yisroel, who have been learning from Hashem, and when they depart [this world], Hashem says to them, "I strived a lot for you."  As it says, (Devarim 1:6), "Hashem our G-d spoke to us at har Sinai, saying, it is enough for you that I rested on this mountain."  So it is, "וענותך תרבני."

Rabbi Shimon said, "a student says to his Rav, 'come teach me one perek,' and the Rav says to him, 'I will wait for you in this place (and he will get there before the student and he will wait for him).'  But Hashem says to Yechezkel (Yechezkel 3:22), "Rise up and come to the valley."  Yechezkel went out, and he found Hashem waiting for him.  As it says, "ואצא אל הבקעה והנה שם כבוד ה' עומד," (when I arrived to the valley, and [already] there stood the kavod (honor) of Hashem.  With this, we say that his [Hashem's] humility is vast....

Lulyani Bar Sibri said in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak:  See the humility that is in the hand of Hashem.  See what it is written there (Shmot 19:19): "Moshe spoke and Hashem answered him b'kol."  It should have been the other way, "Hashem speaks and Moshe answered."  So with this, we see that his [Hashem's] humility is vast.

Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said in the name of Rebbi Shmuel, "See the humility that is in the hand of Hashem [in] what is written (Yechezkel 44:2)," "ויאמר ה' אלי השער הזה סגור יהיה לא יפתח וגו'."  A king of flesh and blood in his honor will enter through a large entrance.  However, Hashem enters in his honor [even] through a small gate.  Thus, His humility is vast.

Ben Azai said, that for a kind of flesh and blood, he is mentioned by his name, however, Hashem is mentioned by what he does, and afterwards, his name is mentioned.  As we see (Bereishit 1:1), "בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ," ['bara' is mentioned before 'Elokim'].

Other examples: "ותתן לי מגן ישעך, אל תירא אברם אנכי מגן לך (Bereishit 15:1). וימינך תסעדני, בכבשן האש, במלכים, וברעבון [דכתיב] נאם ה' לאדוני שב לימיני (Tehillim 110:1)."  From these, we see that Hashem's humility is vast.  We see this also [with Avraham avinu], that he [Avraham] was sitting, and the Shechina was standing, as it says (Bereishit 18:1), "וירא אליו ה' באלוני ממרא והוא יושב פתח האהל."

With all the types of Anava ('humility') that we find down in our world, we find it also with Hashem, which we can compare to the moon.  Just like the moon [is humble] as it diminishes itself and its light, so too with Tzaddikim, as it is explained in mesechet Chullin (page 60:2), "that Hashem calls Tzaddikim by their name, 'Yaakov haKatan' (Yaakov the small), 'Shmuel haKatan,' 'Dovid haKatan' -- Dovid [haMelech] -- who was like a chariot in this attribute diminished his own self worth, as he would says about himself, "I am young and 'nivzeh'." (Tehillim 119:141) While the moon makes itself smaller (just like anything 'kedusha' makes itself smaller), [klipah] makes itself bigger.  Just as it is described in the Zohar (Zohar, parshat Pekudei, page 232:2), "and Dovid haMelech, he lowered himself before Hashem.  And all that lower themselves before Hashem, He will elevate you with everything.  In general, [there is a difference] between this world ('Olam Hazeh') and the next world ('Olam Haba').  In 'Olam Hazeh,' as it says, "וגנותי על העיר הזאת למעני ולמען דוד עבדי," meaning, I planted you here in this city for me and for DOVID MY SERVANT. [In other words, in this world, the reference to greatness is in Dovid haMelech, who was referred to as a SERVANT of Hashem.]  In 'Olam Haba,' as it says (Hoshea 3:5), "ובקשו את ה' אלהיהם ואת דוד מלכם וגו'," [In other words, in the 'Olam Haba,' 'Hashem your G-d' is written as being at the same level as Dovid haMelech.  So humility in our world is lowering one's self; humility in the spiritual world is depicting the person at the level he is at.] Dovid was king in 'Olam Hazeh,' and Dovid was king in 'Olam Haba.'  (In both places, he is considered a king.)  The difference is that in this world, it is said (Tehillim 118:22), "אבן מאסו הבונים היתה לראש פנה," meaning, the stone that is scorned (thrown away) by the builders has become the cornerstone.

Come and see -- when the light of the moon diminishes, and it does not illuminate - there you see its humility (its poverty) in all of its sides.  And when it is created (e.g., 'new moon'), it does not have any light at all.  But when the sun faces [the moon] and shines on it -- there, 'she' (the moon) becomes beautiful, just as the female [wife] beautifies herself for the male [her husband].  Then, [when reflecting the light of the sun] she rules over the world.  So too, Dovid haMelech diminished himself in the same way.  Sometimes he was poor, sometimes he was rich.  Therefore, he used to say, "I am young and of low spirit," and with this, he said [to Hashem], "I did not forget Your commandments." This is the same way that it is for a person who lowers himself in all ways -- so that he can be a vessel (a 'kli') for Hashem who wants him.  And this is how it is, as it says, "ואת דכא ושפל רוח," [meaning, Hashem rests on one who lowers himself].

Therefore, the humble -- whose hearts are broken and crushed -- they are a 'chariot' for this attribute.  And just as it is described in the Zohar (Zohar Parshat Vayikra 9:1), "...but come and see:  Every person in this world is not close to the King Above ('Melech Elyon') unless they are 'kelim' (unless they are a 'kli' or a 'vessel') for Hashem to make use of.  And who are these [who are 'vessels' for Hashem's G-dliness]?  "לב נשבר ונדכה," those whose hearts are broken and crushed (Tehillim 51:19), "ואת דכא ושפל רוח," and those who have a 'shafal ruach' [a small ego] (Yishaya 57:15), these are the vessels of the King.

And so it says in the Midrash (Midrash Vayikra Rabba 80:7) on the passuk of Tehillim (Tehillim 51:19), "זבחי אלהים רוח נשברה," [that the sacrifices to Hashem are a broken spirit], this is what it says.  Rabbi Abba bar Marion says, "כל מה שפסל הקדוש ברוך הוא בבהמה הכשיר באדם," ["all that is passul ('invalid') to Hashem regarding animals is kasher ('kosher') to people."] "Passul in animals," includes, a broken bone, etc. (Vayikra 22:22).  "Kosher for people," refers to a "לב נשבר ונדכה," a broken and crushed heart.  Rabbi Alexsandri explained this -- "if one uses broken vessels, it is not sightly (it is ugly) for him (for a person)."  However, for Hashem, for a vessel to be able to be used [by Him], it [needs to be] broken.  As it says, קרוב ה' לנשברי לב, הרופא לשבורי לב (שם קמו, ג), את דכא ושפל רוח (ישעיה נז, טו), זבחי אלהים רוח נשברה לב נשבר (תהלים נא, יט), etc.  [In other words, we live in an upside-down world.  Everything that is broken to us (when we have a broken heart or a diminished ego), is considered complete to Hashem.  It goes the other way too; many things that we might indulge in, or the act of indulgence itself is not seen as good to Hashem, as the act with desire or pleasure which is not for the sake of a mitzvah falls into klipah and impurity (see Ch 15 of Shaar haKedusha).]

The main character trait of the head is humility, as it is said “low knees” and “pliant to the head”. And this is a person who lowers their head when in the presence of someone who is greater than them, so too the attribute of Keter lowers itself instead of going above all, and that is why it is called “Ayin”, as it thinks of itself as nothing [ayin] in front of the Infuser of Life, and Keter lowers its head to take care and influence the Lower Ones, that all look towards Keter to be sustained by it. And so it is appropriate that a person should think themselves as Ayin [nothing] compared to the greatness of the Holy Blessed One, which has no end or limit, as explained before, and it is regarding that idea that Moshe our teacher, peace be upon him, said “and we, what [are we]?” (Ex. 16:7)
